concepts.title: System
concepts.one_liner: A system is a process or function that transforms a signal into another.
concepts.content: A system is a process or function that transforms a signal into another signal, typically across domains such as time, space, or wavelength.
concepts.motivation_md: In signal processing, we need a way to describe the mechanisms that modify or react to signals. Defining a 'system' provides a mathematical framework for these transformations.

concepts.title: Continuous and Discrete Signals Comparison
concepts.one_liner: Continuous signals in nature are sampled and transformed into finite sequences of numbers called discrete signals for computer processing.
concepts.content:
Although most signals that exist in nature are infinite continuous signals, when we introduce them into a computer they are sampled and transformed into a finite sequence of numbers, also called a discrete signal. As is common in signal processing, we use parentheses to indicate continuous variables and brackets to denote discrete variables. For instance, if we sample the signal shown in @fig-contdiscsignal (a) once every second ($\Delta T = 1$ s) we get the discrete signal shown in @fig-contdiscsignal (b).

(see figure: Fig (a) A continuous signal, and (b) a discrete signal obtained by sampling the continuous signal at the times $t=n$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Computers cannot process infinite, continuous data directly. Sampling allows us to represent real-world phenomena as finite sequences that digital hardware can manipulate.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous signals use parentheses $(t)$ while discrete signals use brackets $[n]$.

concepts.title: Signal Sampling Process
concepts.one_liner: Signal sampling captures values at discrete time instants, such as a camera recording video at 30 frames per second.
concepts.content: If we consider the light that reaches one camera photo sensor, we could write it as a one dimensional function of time, $\ell(t)$, where $\ell(t)$ denotes the incident light at time $t$, and $t$ is a continuous variable that can take on any real value. The signal $\ell(t)$ is then sampled in time by the camera where the values are only captured at discrete times (e.g., 30 times per second). In that case, the signal $\ell$ will be defined only on discrete time instants and we will write the sequence of measured values as: $\ell\left[ n \right]$, where $n$ can only take on integer values.
concepts.motivation_md: Using a camera as an example helps visualize how continuous physical phenomena (light) are captured at specific intervals to create digital data (video frames).
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous signals $\ell(t)$ use real-valued time $t$.

concepts.title: Sampling Equation
concepts.one_liner: The sampling equation $\ell[n] = \ell(n \Delta T)$ relates discrete and continuous signals via the sampling period $\Delta T$.
concepts.content: The relationship between discrete and continuous signals is given by the sampling equation: $$\ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left(n~\Delta T \right)$$ where $\Delta T$ is the sampling period. For instance, $\Delta T = 1/30$ s in the case of sampling a signal 30 times per second.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation provides the mathematical link between a continuous function and its discrete representation, defining exactly which points in time are preserved.

concepts.title: Discrete Signal Vector Notation
concepts.one_liner: Discrete signals can be conveniently represented as column vectors.
concepts.content: In many cases it is convenient to write discrete signals as vectors. Using vector notation, we can write a signal in the interval $n \in \left[0,6 \right]$ as a column vector $\boldsymbol\ell= \left[3, 2, 1, 4, 0, 0, 0\right]^T$, where $T$ denotes transpose. In this example, several values are zero, $\ell\left[n\right] = 0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing signals as vectors allows us to use the powerful tools of linear algebra to process and analyze digital signals.

concepts.title: Systems Overview
concepts.one_liner: A system takes an input signal, performs a computation, and produces an output signal.
concepts.content:
The kind of systems that we will study here take a signal, $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, as input, perform some computation, $f$, and output another signal, $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= f(\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}})$.

(see figure: System processing one signal.)

This transformation is very general and it can do all sorts of complex things: it could detect edges in images, recognize objects, detect motion in sequences, or apply aesthetic transformations to a picture. The function $f$ could be specified as a mathematical operation or as an algorithm. As a consequence, it is very difficult to find a simple way of characterizing what the function $f$ does. In the next section we will study a simple class of functions $f$ that allow for a simple analytical characterization: linear systems.
concepts.motivation_md: Systems provide a mathematical framework for processing signals, such as images. While general systems can be arbitrarily complex, defining them as functions allows us to categorize and analyze specific transformations like edge detection or object recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - A system is a function $f$ that transforms an input signal $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ into an output signal $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}$.

concepts.title: Linear System
concepts.one_liner: A system is linear if it satisfies the properties of additivity and homogeneity.
concepts.content:
Linear systems represent a very small portion of all the possible systems one could implement, but they are capable of creating very interesting image transformations. A function $f$ is linear if it satisfies the following two properties:

$$\begin{aligned}
f\left( \boldsymbol\ell_1+\boldsymbol\ell_2 \right) &=& f(\boldsymbol\ell_1)+ f(\boldsymbol\ell_2) \\ \nonumber
f(a\boldsymbol\ell) &=& af(\boldsymbol\ell) ~~\text{~for any scalar~} a
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity simplifies the analysis of complex systems by allowing us to decompose inputs and study their effects independently. This property is foundational for many image processing techniques.
concepts.recap_md: - Linearity requires additivity: $f(\ell_1 + \ell_2) = f(\ell_1) + f(\ell_2)$.

concepts.title: Linear System Matrix Formulation
concepts.one_liner: A linear system can be expressed as a matrix-vector multiplication where the output is a linear combination of input values.
concepts.content:
To make things more concrete, assume the input is a 1D signal with length $N$ written as $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$, and the output is another 1D signal with length $M$ written as $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right]$. Most of the times we will work with input and output pairs with the same length $M=N$. A linear system, in its most general form, can be written as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[n,k\right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right] ~~~ for ~~~ n \in \left[0, M-1 \right]
$$ where each output value $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right]$ is a linear combination of values of the input signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ with weights $h \left[n,k\right]$. The value $h \left[n,k\right]$ is the weight applied to the input sample $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$ to compute the output sample $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right]$. To help visualizing the operation performed by the linear filter it is useful to write it in matrix form:
$$\begin{bmatrix}\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 0 \right] \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 1 \right] \\
\vdots \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ n \right] \\
\vdots \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ M-1 \right]
\end{bmatrix}
 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  h\left[0,0\right] ~&~ h\left[0,1\right] ~&~ ... ~&~ h\left[0,N-1\right] \\
  h\left[1,0\right] ~&~ h\left[1,1\right] ~&~ ... ~&~ h\left[1,N-1\right] \\
  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots \\
  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  h \left[n,k\right] ~&~  \vdots \\
\vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots \\
  h\left[M-1,0\right] ~&~ h\left[M-1,1\right] ~&~ ... ~&~ h\left[M-1,N-1\right] 
 \end{bmatrix}
~
 \begin{bmatrix}
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[0\right] \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[1\right] \\
  \vdots \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k\right] \\
  \vdots \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[N-1\right]
 \end{bmatrix}$$
which we will write in short form as $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$. The matrix $\mathbf{H}$ has size $M \times N$.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing linear systems as matrices allows us to use the powerful tools of linear algebra to analyze and implement signal transformations efficiently.

concepts.title: 2D Linear Systems
concepts.one_liner: In 2D, linear systems compute output pixels as a linear combination of input pixels, often represented by flattening images into vectors.
concepts.content:
In two dimensions the equations are analogous. Each pixel of the output image, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right]$, is computed as a linear combination of pixels of the input image, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n, m\right]$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} \sum_{l=0}^{N-1} h \left[n,m,k,l \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k,l \right]
$$ By writing the images as column vectors, concatenating all the image columns into a long vector, we can also write the previous equation using matrices and vectors: $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Extending linear systems to 2D is essential for image processing, where data is naturally organized in grids rather than 1D sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - 2D linear systems use double summations to process pixel grids.

concepts.title: Linear Translation Invariant (LTI) System
concepts.one_liner: Linear translation invariant (LTI) systems apply the same processing algorithm at every spatial position.
concepts.content:
Linear systems are still too general for us. So let's consider an even smaller family of systems: **linear translation invariant** (LTI) **systems**.

[FIGURE:b7749e9467b10dd1 | A Venn diagram showing nested subsets of mathematical functions. The largest set is 'All functions' (red), which contains 'Differentiable' functions (yellow), which in turn contains 'Linear'...]

Translation invariant systems are motivated by the following observation: typically, we don't know where within the image we expect to find any given item, so we often want to process the image in a spatially invariant manner, the same processing algorithm at every pixel.
concepts.motivation_md: Since objects can appear anywhere in an image, it is efficient and logical to use systems that treat all spatial locations identically.
concepts.recap_md: - LTI systems are a subset of linear systems that are spatially invariant.

concepts.title: Translation Equivariance
concepts.one_liner: A system is translation equivariant if translating the input results in a corresponding translation of the output.
concepts.content:
A system is an LTI system if it is linear and when we translate the input signal by $n_0, m_0$, then output is also translated by $n_0, m_0$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ n - n_0, m-m_0 \right] = f \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[ n-n_0, m-m_0 \right] \right)$$
for any $n_0,m_0$. This property is called **equivariant** with respect to translation. Translation invariance and linearity impose a strong constraint on the form of the general linear filter equation.
concepts.motivation_md: Equivariance ensures that the system's response is consistent regardless of where the input signal is located in the domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation equivariance means $f(\text{shifted input}) = \text{shifted output}$.

concepts.title: Convolution and Convolution Kernel
concepts.one_liner: An LTI system can be expressed as a convolution of the input data with a convolution kernel.
concepts.content: In the case of a linear translation invariant system, the linear system becomes a **convolution** of the image data with some **convolution kernel**. This operation is very important and we devote the rest of this chapter to study its properties.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution provides a computationally efficient and mathematically elegant way to implement LTI systems.

concepts.title: Associative Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolutions can be applied in any order, allowing the grouping of multiple kernels or signals without changing the result.
concepts.content:
Convolutions are associative, meaning they can be applied in any order:
$$\ell_1 [n] \circ \ell_2 [n] \circ \ell_3 [n] = \ell_1[n] \circ (\ell_2[n] \circ \ell_3[n]) = (\ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n]) \circ \ell_3[n]$$
In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by how boundary conditions are implemented.
concepts.motivation_md: Associativity allows for the pre-computation of multiple filters into a single equivalent kernel, which can significantly improve computational efficiency in signal processing and neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution is associative, meaning $(\ell_1 \circ \ell_2) \circ \ell_3 = \ell_1 \circ (\ell_2 \circ \ell_3)$.

slots.key_passage: - Convolution is associative, meaning $(\ell_1 \circ \ell_2) \circ \ell_3 = \ell_1 \circ (\ell_2 \circ \ell_3)$.

concepts.title: Distributive Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution is distributive with respect to addition, allowing a kernel to be applied to a sum of signals individually.
concepts.content:
Convolution is distributive with respect to the sum:
$$\ell_1[n] \circ (\ell_2[n] + \ell_3[n] ) = \ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n] +  \ell_1 [n] \circ \ell_3 [n]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property ensures that filtering a combined signal is the same as filtering each component separately and then adding them, which is fundamental to linear system theory.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution distributes over addition: $f \circ (g + h) = f \circ g + f \circ h$.

concepts.title: Shift Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Translating either the input signal or the kernel by a constant results in an output translated by that same constant.
concepts.content:
Another interesting property involves shifting the two convolved functions. Consider the convolution $\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n] = h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$. If the input signal, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$, is translated by a constant $n_0$, i.e. $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n - n_0]$, the result of the convolution with the same kernel, $h[n]$, is the same output as before but translated by the same constant $n_0$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n-n_0] =  h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n-n_0]$$

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n-n_0] =  h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n-n_0]  = h[n-n_0] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$$

concepts.title: Convolution Identity (Impulse)
concepts.one_liner: The impulse function $\delta[n]$ acts as the identity for convolution, returning the original signal unchanged.

concepts.one_liner: Boundary handling addresses the ambiguity of computing convolution values where the kernel overlaps the edge of the input signal.

concepts.title: Zero Padding
concepts.one_liner: Zero padding sets pixels outside the signal boundary to zero or another constant to maintain output size.

concepts.title: Circular Padding
concepts.one_liner: Circular padding extends a signal by replicating pixels from the opposite side, treating the signal as periodic.
concepts.content:
Circular padding extends the image by replicating the pixels from the other side. If the image has size $P \times Q$, circular padding consists of the following:
$$\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n,m] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}[(n)_P,(m)_Q]$$
where $(n)_P$ denotes the modulo operation and $(n)_P$ is the reminder of $n/P$.

This padding transforms the finite length signal into a periodic infinite length signal. Although this will introduce many artifacts, it is a convenient extension for analytical derivations.
concepts.motivation_md: Circular padding is mathematically useful because it aligns with the properties of the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), where signals are inherently treated as periodic.

concepts.title: Signal Length Classification
concepts.one_liner: Signals are classified as infinite length if they extend over the entire support or finite length if they are zero outside a compact interval.
concepts.content: Both continuous and discrete signals can be classified according to their extent. **Infinite length** signals are signals that extend over the entire support $\ell\left[n \right]$ for $n \in (-\infty, \infty)$. **Finite length** signals have non-zero values on a compact time interval and they are zero outside, i.e. $\ell\left[n \right] = 0$ for $n \notin S$ where $S$ is a finite length interval.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between finite and infinite signals is crucial for determining which mathematical tools (like specific transforms or summation methods) are applicable and for understanding the memory requirements of a signal.

concepts.title: Periodic Signal

concepts.motivation_md: Periodicity is a fundamental property in signal processing that allows us to represent complex signals as sums of simpler oscillating components, such as in Fourier analysis.

concepts.title: DC Value
concepts.one_liner: The DC value is the mean value of a signal, representing the average intensity in the case of an image.
concepts.content: The mean value of a signal is often called the **DC value**. DC means **direct current** and it comes from electrical engineering. Although most signals have nothing to do with currents, the term DC is still commonly used. In the case of an image, the DC component is the average intensity of the image. For a finite signal of length $N$ (or a periodic signal), the **DC value** is $$\mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \ell\left[n\right]$$ If the signal is infinite, the average value is $$\mu = \lim_{N \xrightarrow{} \infty} \frac{1}{2N+1} \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \ell\left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The DC value represents the baseline or 'offset' of a signal. In image processing, it corresponds to the overall brightness, and separating it from the 'AC' (varying) components is a key step in many compression and enhancement algorithms.

concepts.title: Energy of a Signal
concepts.one_liner: The energy of a signal is defined as the sum of its squared magnitude values.
concepts.content: The **energy of a signal** is defined as the sum of squared magnitude values: $$E = \sum_{n = -\infty}^{\infty} \left| \ell\left[n\right] \right| ^2$$ Signal energy and general energy are equivalent up to a normalization constant. For instance, the energy dissipated by a resistance $R$ with voltage $v(t)$ is \begin{equation} E = \frac{1}{R} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} v(t) ^2 dt \end{equation} Signals are further classified as **finite energy** and **infinite energy** signals. Finite length signals are finite energy and periodic signals are infinite energy signals when measuring the energy in the whole time axis.

concepts.title: Squared Euclidean Distance for Signals
concepts.one_liner: The squared Euclidean distance (L2 norm) is used to compare two signals by summing the squared differences of their values.

concepts.one_liner: Circular convolution uses circular padding to convolve a finite length signal by treating it as an infinite periodic extension.

This trick is also very useful analytically and leads to a special case: the circular convolution, which uses circular padding. The circular convolution of two signals, $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, of length $N$ is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$ In this formulation, the signal $h \left[ (n)_N \right]$ is the infinite periodic extension, with period $N$, of the finite length signal $h \left[n \right]$. The output of the circular convolution is a periodic signal with period $N$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[(n)_N \right]$. The circular convolution has the same properties as standard convolution, such as being commutative.

concepts.title: Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Cross-correlation is a translation-invariant operator used to locate templates in an image without inverting the kernel.
concepts.content: The cross-correlation operator provides a simple technique to locate a template in an image and is closely related to convolution. The cross-correlation operator (denoted by $\star$) between the image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and the kernel $h$ is written as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$ where the sum is performed over the support of the filter $h$, assumed to be a square $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$. In the convolution, the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, while in the cross-correlation it is not. For comparison, the convolution between image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and kernel $h$ is: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\circ h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-k,m-l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-correlation is primarily used for template matching, as it measures the similarity between a kernel and different parts of an image without the need for the kernel flipping required by convolution.

- Used to locate templates within a larger image.
- Unlike convolution, the kernel $h$ is not inverted (flipped) during the operation.
- Mathematically defined as $\sum \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n+k, m+l] h[k, l]$.

concepts.title: Normalized Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Normalized cross-correlation is the dot product between a zero-mean, unit-norm template and a unit-norm local image patch, providing invariance to local intensity changes.
concepts.content: The normalized cross-correlation at location $(n,m)$ is the dot product between a template $h$ (normalized to be zero mean and unit norm) and the local image patch $p$ centered at that location, which is normalized to be unit norm. This can be implemented by first normalizing the kernel $h$ to obtain $\hat h$ with zero mean and unit norm. The normalized cross-correlation is then given by (@fig-normcorr (d)): $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma \left[n,m \right]} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] \hat{h} \left[k,l \right]$$ This equation is similar to the correlation function, but the output is scaled by the local standard deviation, $\sigma \left[m,n \right]$, of the image patch centered in $(n,m)$ and with support $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$, where $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$ is the size of the kernel $h$. To compute the local standard deviation, we first compute the local mean, $\mu \left[n,m \right]$, as follows: $$\mu \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{(2N+1)^2} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right]$$ And then we compute: $$\sigma^2 \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{(2N+1)^2} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] - \mu \left[n,m \right] \right) ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: Normalized cross-correlation is used for template matching because it is robust against changes in lighting and contrast. By normalizing both the template and the local image patch, the matching process becomes invariant to local intensity scaling.

concepts.title: System Identification
concepts.one_liner: System identification is the process of finding the convolution kernel of an unknown LTI system by computing its output when the input is an impulse.
concepts.content: One important task is explaining the behavior of complex systems such as neural networks. For an LTI filter with kernel $h\left[n\right]$, the output from an impulse is $y\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right]$. The output of a translated impulse $\delta \left[n -n_0 \right]$ is $h \left[n -n_0 \right]$. This is why the kernel that defines an LTI system, $h\left[n\right]$, is also called the impulse response of the system. For an unknown system, one way of finding the convolution kernel $h$ consists in computing the output of the system when the input is an impulse.
concepts.motivation_md: System identification allows us to characterize and model complex or unknown systems by observing their response to a simple impulse, which completely defines the behavior of any Linear Time-Invariant system.

concepts.title: Acoustic Impulse Response of a Room
concepts.one_liner: The acoustic impulse response of a room models how sound is distorted by echoes based on the room's geometry and materials.
concepts.content: In acoustics, sounds in a room are often distorted with echoes, the number and strength of which depend on the geometry of the room, its contents, and the materials in the walls and ceilings. (see figure: As shown in the sketch, sounds produced by one speaking person reach a listener via multiple paths. What the person hears is the superposition of all those signals. A clap serves as a good approximation to an impulse of sound; the echoes heard are very close to the impulse response of the system formed by the room's acoustics. (see figure: Fig (a) Apparatus used to measure the impulse response generated by a battery-powered speaker and a portable digital recorder. (b) Recorded acoustic impulse response of a room. Figure modified from...) The impulse response, $h (t)$, can be modeled as a sequence of impulses representing different paths with specific delays ($T_i$) and amplitudes ($a_i$): $$h (t) = a_0 \delta (t) + a_1 \delta \left(t-T_1 \right) + a_2 \delta \left( t-T_2 \right) + a_3 \delta \left( t-T_3 \right)$$ The sound that reaches the listener is the convolution of the input sound, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, with the room impulse response, $h (t)$: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) \circ h(t) = a_0 \ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) + a_1 \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t-T_1) + a_2 \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t-T_2) + a_3 \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t-T_3)$$ (see figure: Modified from @TraerE7856.)

concepts.title: Relationship between Convolution and Correlation

concepts.one_liner: Convolution is commutative, meaning the order of the signal and the kernel does not affect the resulting output.
concepts.content: One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative: $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$. This property is easy to prove by changing the variables, $k = n - k'$, so that: $$h \left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[n-k \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right] = \sum_{k'=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[k' \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-k' \right]  = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] \circ h \left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Commutativity provides mathematical flexibility, allowing the kernel and signal to be treated interchangeably in proofs and system analysis.

concepts.title: Procedural Steps of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution is performed by mirroring the kernel, shifting it to the target location, multiplying by the input, and summing the results.
concepts.content: The convolution operation can be described procedurally: first take the kernel $h\left[k\right]$ and mirror it $h\left[-k \right]$, then shift the mirrored kernel so that the origin is at location $n$, then multiply the input values around location $n$ by the mirrored kernel and sum the result. Store the result in the output vector $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$. For instance, if the convolutional kernel has three non-zero values: $h\left[-1 \right] =1$, $h\left[0 \right] = 2$ and $h\left[1 \right] = 3$, then the output value at location $n$ is $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = 3 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-1\right]+2 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] + 1 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+1\right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: A procedural understanding provides a clear algorithmic path for manual calculation or software implementation of the convolution operation.
concepts.recap_md: - The process involves mirroring the kernel, shifting it, multiplying, and summing.

concepts.title: Convolution in Matrix Form
concepts.one_liner: For finite signals, convolution can be represented as a matrix-vector multiplication using a structured matrix derived from the kernel.
concepts.content: For finite length signals, the structure of the convolution can be made explicit by writing it in matrix form. For instance, if the convolutional kernel has only three non-zero values, then: $$\begin{bmatrix} \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 0 \right] \\ \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 1 \right] \\ \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 2 \right] \\ \vdots \\ \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ N-1 \right] \end{bmatrix}  = \begin{bmatrix}   h\left[0\right] ~&~ h\left[-1\right] ~&~ 0 ~&~ ... ~&~ 0 \\   h\left[1\right] ~&~ h\left[0\right] ~&~ h\left[-1\right] ~&~... ~&~ 0 \\   0 ~&~ h\left[1\right] ~&~ h\left[0\right] ~&~... ~&~ 0 \\   \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots \\   0 ~&~ 0 ~&~ 0 ~&~... ~&~ h\left[0\right]   \end{bmatrix} ~  \begin{bmatrix}   \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[0\right] \\   \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[1\right] \\   \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[2\right] \\   \vdots \\   \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[N-1\right]  \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing convolution in matrix form allows for the application of linear algebra tools and efficient computation using optimized numerical libraries.
concepts.recap_md: - Finite convolution can be expressed as a matrix-vector product $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Convolutional Layer
concepts.one_liner: A convolutional layer in a neural network computes outputs as local linear combinations of inputs using shared weights.
concepts.content: Convolution is often represented as a layer within a neural network. In this view, each output unit $i$, denoted $\ell_{\text{out}}[i]$, is a linear combination of the input signal values surrounding location $i$, consistently using the same set of weights $\mathbf{h}$.  ![ convolution represented as a layer in a neural network. concepts.title: 2D Convolution
concepts.one_liner: 2D convolution involves flipping a kernel in both dimensions and sliding it over an image to compute local inner products.
concepts.content: In two dimensions, the processing is analogous: the input filter is flipped vertically and horizontally, then slid over the image to record the inner product with the image everywhere. prereq.rationale: Systems Overview builds on the general definition of a system to describe signal processing transformations.
Linear systems are introduced as a specific, analytically simple class of the general systems described in the overview.
The matrix formulation is a concrete mathematical representation of the abstract properties of a linear system.
Expressing a linear system as a matrix-vector product requires representing discrete signals as vectors.
The fully connected layer representation directly uses the matrix H from the linear system's matrix formulation.
Applying linear systems to 2D requires the definition of an image as a 2D discrete signal.
LTI systems are defined as a specific subset of linear systems that also possess translation invariance.
Convolution is the fundamental operation that characterizes all linear translation invariant systems.
The convolution operation arises specifically from the constraint of translation equivariance on a linear system.
System identification as described here specifically aims to find the convolution kernel that characterizes a Linear Translation Invariant system.
The technique relies on the property that the output of a system is its kernel when the input is an impulse.
The impulse response is defined as the output of an LTI system when the input is an impulse.
The concept of an impulse response is the physical manifestation of the impulse being the identity element for convolution.
Modeling room acoustics as an impulse response assumes the relationship between sound source and listener is an LTI system.
Cross-correlation is defined in the context of its close relationship to convolution, sharing a similar mathematical structure.
Cross-correlation is a translation-invariant operator, a property that allows it to detect features regardless of their position in the image.
The technique of template matching relies on the cross-correlation operator to measure the similarity between a template and image patches.
Normalized cross-correlation is an extension of the cross-correlation operator that includes scaling by local image statistics.
